people.name: William H. Reitz
people.summary: Xylophone and bells soloist of the 1910s, heard on Victor and Edison and in the house orchestras of both.
people.biography:
William H. Reitz was one of the studio percussionists whose xylophone solos and obbligatos are scattered across the American catalogues of the 1910s. He recorded solos for Victor and Edison and played in their house orchestras, where the xylophone was used both as a novelty voice and as a practical way of adding definition to an acoustically recorded ensemble.

His solo records — rags, marches and light novelties — appear among four-minute cylinder issues and share the bright, immediate quality that makes acoustic xylophone recordings unexpectedly satisfying to listen to today.

people.name: Charles D'Almaine
people.summary: One of the first violinists ever recorded, later concertmaster of the Victor Orchestra, and a prolific cylinder soloist.
people.biography:
Charles D'Almaine was an English-born violinist who played with the Metropolitan Opera orchestra and became one of the earliest violinists to make commercial records — his first, a "Miserere," was cut in 1899 and issued as Edison cylinder 7324. He joined Victor in 1901 and eventually became concertmaster of the house orchestra there.

The violin was a difficult instrument for acoustic recording — thin and wiry through the horn, which is why Stroh violins with metal resonators were used in some studios — and D'Almaine's success says a good deal about his tone and his understanding of the medium. He recorded hornpipes, medleys, salon pieces and light classics, and his material appears on both two-minute and four-minute cylinders. He later practised as a chiropractor. He died on 17 June 1943.

people.name: Bohumir Kryl
people.summary: Czech-American cornet virtuoso and bandmaster, billed as 'the Caruso of the Cornet', and a favourite of the cylinder catalogues.
people.biography:
Bohumir Kryl was born in Bohemia on 3 May 1875 and arrived in the United States as a teenager, working — by his own colourful account — as an acrobat and a sculptor's assistant before his cornet playing was discovered. He played with Sousa's Band and with Innes's Band before forming his own touring band, which was among the most successful in America in the 1900s and 1910s.

His technique was formidable: double and triple tonguing, a huge range, and the kind of showy variation-on-a-theme solo that a brass virtuoso of the period was expected to produce. Cornet solos recorded superbly by the acoustic process, and Kryl's records for Columbia, Victor and the cylinder companies sold in quantity. His band and solo material appears on four-minute cylinders, including on Indestructible.

He later prospered in business and became a serious art collector. He died on 7 August 1961.

people.name: Herbert L. Clarke
people.summary: The most celebrated cornet soloist of the band era, long a featured artist with Sousa's Band and a composer of the instrument's standard showpieces.
people.biography:
Herbert Lincoln Clarke was born on 12 September 1867 and became the defining cornet virtuoso of the American band tradition. He was soloist and later assistant conductor with Sousa's Band over a period of two decades, and his own compositions — "The Debutante," "Bride of the Waves," "Sounds from the Hudson," "From the Shores of the Mighty Pacific" — remain the standard test pieces for cornet players a century later.

His recorded solos, made for Victor, Columbia and the cylinder companies, show a clean, warm tone and a fluency in double and triple tonguing that has rarely been matched. Because brass recorded so well acoustically, cornet solos were a staple of every cylinder catalogue, and Clarke's are the finest of them. He later conducted bands in Huntsville and Long Beach and wrote a set of technical studies still in universal use. He died on 30 January 1945.

people.name: John J. Kimmel
people.summary: German-American master of the one-row diatonic accordion whose Irish dance recordings shaped traditional Irish music in America.
people.biography:
John J. Kimmel was born in Brooklyn in 1866 to German parents and became, improbably, one of the most influential performers of Irish traditional dance music ever recorded. He played the one-row diatonic button accordion with a clarity of ornament and a rhythmic lift that Irish musicians on both sides of the Atlantic studied and copied.

His earliest recordings were Edison wax cylinders around 1906, and he went on to record for Victor, Columbia, Zon-o-phone and the cylinder labels through the 1910s and into the 1920s. Reels, jigs and hornpipes were his stock in trade, along with marches and popular medleys. His records circulated widely in Irish-American communities and are a foundation document of the recorded Irish tradition.

He died in 1942. His name is spelled variously on labels, including as Kimmble, which is worth knowing when searching a catalogue.

people.name: Guido Deiro
people.summary: The first piano-accordionist to headline American vaudeville and to record commercially, and the man who made the instrument popular in the United States.
people.biography:
Guido Deiro was born in Salto Canavese, Italy, on 1 September 1886 and came to the United States in 1907. He was the first piano-accordion soloist on big-time American vaudeville, the first to record commercially, and the first to broadcast — a genuine pioneer whose success created a market for the instrument that lasted half a century.

He recorded for Columbia from 1911 and later for other labels, in Italian dances, operatic transcriptions, rags and his own compositions such as "Sharpshooters' March" and "Kismet." His material appears on four-minute cylinders through Columbia's Indestructible issues. He was briefly married to Mae West. He died on 26 July 1950; his younger brother Pietro carried the family name forward for another four years.

people.name: Pietro Deiro
people.summary: Guido Deiro's younger brother, one of the most influential accordionists of the first half of the twentieth century and a prolific recording artist.
people.biography:
Pietro Deiro was born in Salto Canavese, Italy, on 28 August 1888 and followed his elder brother Guido to America. He became a vaudeville headliner in his own right and recorded prolifically for Victor and Columbia from the 1910s, in Italian folk material, marches, operatic transcriptions and his own compositions.

He was later known as the "Daddy of the Accordion" for his work as a teacher, publisher and advocate of the instrument, and his method books trained several generations of American players. His recordings reached four-minute cylinder buyers through Columbia's Indestructible line. He died in 1954.

people.name: Eugene C. Rose
people.summary: Flute and piccolo soloist, a member of Sousa's Band at the turn of the century and a regular Edison recording artist.
people.biography:
Eugene C. Rose played flute and piccolo with Sousa's Band around 1900–1902 and recorded piccolo solos for Edison from about the same period. The piccolo was another instrument that suited the acoustic horn — piercing, high and full of transient detail — and piccolo solos with orchestra were a standing category in every cylinder catalogue.

Rose's polkas, variations and novelty pieces were issued on Edison cylinders and were remade or carried forward into the four-minute format. He also played in Edison's studio orchestra.

people.name: Charles Schuetze
people.summary: Harpist whose solos are among the few recorded harp records of the acoustic cylinder era.
people.biography:
Charles Schuetze was one of the very small number of harpists to record commercially in the acoustic period. The harp was a difficult proposition for the recording horn — quiet, diffuse and rich in exactly the overtones the process lost — and harp records are correspondingly scarce and prized.

Schuetze recorded solos and accompaniments for Edison, and his material appears among cylinder issues of the 1900s and 1910s. He also played in ensembles such as the Ossman-Dudley Trio's harp-guitar tradition of plucked-string combinations, though the harp itself remained an unusual sound on record.

people.name: Samuel Siegel
people.summary: The leading American mandolin virtuoso of the early recording era, admired for a legato tremolo unusual on the instrument.
people.biography:
Samuel Siegel was the outstanding American mandolinist of the period around 1900–1915, a player whose tremolo was smooth enough to sustain a genuine melodic line and whose arrangements raised the mandolin above its usual status as a parlour novelty. He recorded for Edison, Victor and Columbia, solo and in duet with guitarists and banjoists.

Plucked strings recorded well acoustically, and mandolin solos were a regular feature of cylinder catalogues. Siegel's records are the best of them, and his four-minute issues gave him room for the extended variation sets he favoured.

people.name: Joe Belmont
people.summary: 'The Human Bird' — the best-known American whistling artist of the early phonograph, and a baritone besides.
people.biography:
Joe Belmont was the stage name of Joseph Walter Fulton, born 22 July 1876, who became the most successful of the whistling recording artists at a time when whistling was a serious professional speciality. Billed as "The Human Bird," he recorded whistling solos with orchestra and piano from the 1890s onward and was among the best-selling artists on record before 1900.

He was also a competent baritone and sang with the Columbia Quartet. Whistling was ideally suited to acoustic recording — a clean, pure, sharply focused tone with almost no wasted energy — and whistling records remained a catalogue staple well into the four-minute era. Belmont recorded for Edison, Columbia, Victor and the cylinder labels. He died on 29 August 1949.

people.name: Sibyl Sanderson Fagan
people.summary: Whistling soloist and bird imitator who recorded for Columbia, Edison, Victor and OKeh from about 1917 into the 1920s.
people.biography:
Sibyl Sanderson Fagan was one of the last of the professional whistling artists to build a substantial recording career. She recorded from about 1917 for Columbia and subsequently for OKeh, Edison and Victor, in whistling solos, bird imitations and novelty pieces such as "The Boy and the Birds" and "The Little Whistler."

The whistling craze that had begun in the 1890s with performers like Alice Shaw was fading by the mid-1920s, and Fagan's recording career ended with it. Her Edison sides reached four-minute cylinder buyers on Blue Amberol, and she is one of the few women in the whistling category, which had otherwise become male-dominated.

people.name: Guido Gialdini
people.summary: European art-whistler of remarkable accuracy, widely issued in America including on Indestructible four-minute cylinders.
people.biography:
Guido Gialdini was a *Kunstpfeifer* — an art whistler — who built an international career on an ability to whistle operatic coloratura and light-classical showpieces with the precision of a flute. He recorded in Europe from the mid-1900s and his records were issued in America as well.

His repertoire ran to Arditi's "Il Bacio," excerpts from *La Traviata*, waltzes and character pieces, and his intonation and breath control were extraordinary. Indestructible issued him on four-minute cylinders, and his records are among the more surprising things a collector will find in a cylinder box — a reminder that whistling was a recognised concert speciality, not a novelty.
people.notes: Sources give his real name as Kurt Abramowitsch and his origin as German; this is repeated in several places but not independently verified here.

people.name: Charles Kellogg
people.summary: 'The Nature Singer' — a vaudeville bird imitator of uncanny accuracy and, later, a campaigner for the California redwoods.
people.biography:
Charles Kellogg was born on 2 October 1868 and grew up in the Sierra Nevada foothills, where he claimed to have learned birdsong before he learned speech. He could reproduce bird calls with a fidelity that astonished ornithologists, and he insisted that he produced them not by whistling but with the syrinx-like use of his own throat.

He toured vaudeville as "The Nature Singer" and recorded for Victor and Edison between 1915 and the mid-1920s, issuing programmes of native birdsong. His Edison material reached four-minute cylinder buyers on Blue Amberol. He also performed a celebrated demonstration in which he extinguished a flame with a sustained tone from a violin, and he spent his later years touring in a truck built from a hollowed redwood log to campaign for the preservation of the forests. He died on 5 September 1949.

people.name: Frank Ferera
people.summary: The first star of recorded Hawaiian music and one of the most recorded guitarists of the acoustic era.
people.biography:
Frank Ferera was born in Honolulu and came to the American mainland in the wake of the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition, which set off a national craze for Hawaiian music that lasted a decade. Between about 1915 and 1930 he became the most recorded Hawaiian musician in the world, working for Victor, Columbia, Edison, Brunswick and a long list of smaller labels.

He played steel guitar in a sweet, gliding, heavily portamento style that defined the popular idea of Hawaiian music for a generation and fed directly into the development of the steel guitar in country music. He recorded with his wife Helen Louise, with Anthony Franchini, and behind singers including Ernest Hare and Al Bernard.

His Edison sides were issued on Diamond Disc and dubbed to Blue Amberol, and Hawaiian selections are a substantial category in the late four-minute cylinder catalogue.

people.name: Helen Louise
people.summary: Guitarist who recorded a long series of Hawaiian duets with Frank Ferera, her husband, in the late 1910s.
people.biography:
Helen Louise recorded as the duet partner of Frank Ferera during the peak of the Hawaiian music craze, and the credit "Louise and Ferera" appears on a large number of records issued between roughly 1915 and 1919 by Victor, Columbia, Edison and others.

The pair's guitar duets — one playing steel, one rhythm — established the standard texture of commercial Hawaiian records. Her career ended with her death in 1919, and Ferera continued with other partners.
people.notes: Accounts of her death at sea in 1919 are widely repeated but the details vary between sources.

people.name: Edna White
people.summary: Pioneering woman trumpet soloist who recorded for Edison, both alone and with her trumpet quartet.
people.biography:
Edna White was one of the very few women to make a career as a brass soloist in the early twentieth century. A cornet and trumpet virtuoso trained at the Institute of Musical Art in New York, she toured in concert, played for troops in France during the First World War, and led the Edna White Trumpet Quartet.

She recorded for Edison, and her solos and quartet numbers were issued on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol cylinder. Brass reproduced exceptionally well acoustically, which makes her records both historically notable and unusually good listening.

people.name: American Quartet
people.summary: The most successful male close-harmony group of the acoustic era, led by Billy Murray; the same singers recorded for Edison as the Premier Quartet.
people.biography:
The American Quartet was assembled at Victor in 1909 around Billy Murray, and in its classic form comprised John Bieling (first tenor), Murray (second tenor and lead), Steve Porter (baritone) and William F. Hooley (bass). Between 1909 and 1913 that line-up made a series of records — "Casey Jones," "Oh! You Beautiful Doll," "Moonlight Bay," "Come, Josephine, in My Flying Machine," "It's a Long Way to Tipperary" — that were among the best-selling American records of the entire acoustic period.

Because of exclusivity arrangements the same men recorded for Edison under the name **Premier Quartet** (or Quartette), and the two names should be understood as one group. On four-minute cylinders they appear on Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol as the Premier Quartet, and elsewhere under further variants.

Membership shifted over the years — Bieling retired in 1913 with vocal trouble, Hooley died in 1918, and Albert Campbell, John Young, Donald Chalmers, John H. Meyer and Frank Croxton all passed through — but Murray remained the constant and the sound remained recognisable: fast, bright, rhythmically snappy, and built for comedy rather than sentiment. The group wound down in the mid-1920s.

people.name: Premier Quartet
people.summary: The name under which the American Quartet recorded for Edison — the same singers, a different label credit.
people.biography:
Premier Quartet is the name Edison printed on cylinders and discs made by the group known at Victor as the American Quartet. The practice was routine: a company under an exclusive contract could not credit a rival's house group by its familiar name, so it invented one.

Under this billing Billy Murray and his colleagues recorded a large body of Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol cylinders through the 1910s — comic songs, marches, patriotic numbers and the popular hits of the day. Anyone cataloguing four-minute cylinders will meet the Premier Quartet constantly, and should read it as the American Quartet in Edison clothing.

A separate entry is kept here because the credit appears on labels in its own right and collectors search for it as printed.
people.notes: Same personnel as the American Quartet; treated as a distinct credit because the name is what appears on Edison labels.

people.name: Peerless Quartet
people.summary: The longest-lived male quartet of the acoustic era, founded by Frank C. Stanley and later run by Henry Burr, and the standard voice of the sentimental and patriotic song.
people.biography:
The Peerless Quartet began around 1904 as the Columbia Male Quartette, organised by the bass Frank C. Stanley, and took the Peerless name a few years later. Its early membership included Stanley, Albert Campbell, Henry Burr and Steve Porter. After Stanley's death in 1910 Henry Burr took over the management and the group continued, with changing personnel — John H. Meyer, Arthur Collins, Frank Croxton and others — until 1928.

Where the American Quartet was fast and comic, the Peerless was the group you engaged for a ballad, a hymn or a patriotic number. They recorded for every major company and are ubiquitous on four-minute cylinders: Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Indestructible, Columbia Indestructible and U-S Everlasting. Their wartime records — "Over There," "It's a Long, Long Way to Tipperary" and dozens of similar titles — were among the biggest sellers of 1917 and 1918.

No other American vocal group of the period recorded for so long or so widely, which makes the Peerless Quartet one of the essential names for anyone working through a four-minute catalogue.

people.name: Haydn Quartet
people.summary: Formed in 1896 as the Edison Quartet, the group that made close harmony a commercial staple — and the voices on 'Sweet Adeline' and 'In the Good Old Summer Time'.
people.biography:
The Haydn Quartet was formed in 1896 as the **Edison Quartet**, to record for the National Phonograph Company, and adopted the Haydn name — a nod to Joseph Haydn — when the same four men recorded for other companies. The spelling was later altered to Hayden, closer to how audiences pronounced it.

The founding line-up was John Bieling (first tenor), Jere Mahoney (second tenor), S. H. Dudley, in real life Samuel Holland Rous (baritone), and William F. Hooley (bass); Mahoney was soon replaced by Harry Macdonough, whose smooth lead defined the group's sound for the rest of its life. Their records — "Sweet Adeline," "In the Good Old Summer Time," "Take Me Out to the Ball Game," "Shine On, Harvest Moon" — were among the most popular of the century's first decade and effectively created the market for barbershop-style harmony on record.

Most of their cylinder work belongs to the two-minute period; a good deal of it was remade or dubbed for four-minute issue, and the group's repertoire remained in Edison and Victor catalogues long after they stopped recording. They disbanded in 1914.

people.name: Edison Mixed Quartet
people.summary: Edison's house ensemble of soprano, contralto, tenor and bass, used chiefly for sacred music, part-songs and light classics.
people.biography:
The Edison Mixed Quartet was the company's standing four-voice ensemble of mixed voices — soprano, contralto, tenor and bass — drawn from its house singers and used for the repertoire a male quartet could not cover: hymns and sacred part-songs, arrangements of folk material, glees, and light classical selections such as the quartet from *Rigoletto*.

Its membership varied with whoever was on the Edison payroll, and it was billed at different periods as the Metropolitan Quartet. Mixed-voice sacred records were a substantial commercial category, sold to a market that would not buy popular songs, and they appear throughout the Amberol and Blue Amberol catalogues.
people.notes: Edison used the Mixed Quartet and Metropolitan Quartet billings for what was largely the same pool of house singers; the two credits are not always cleanly distinguishable.

people.name: Metropolitan Quartet
people.summary: Edison mixed-voice ensemble credit, used for sacred and part-song material on Blue Amberol cylinders and Diamond Discs.
people.biography:
The Metropolitan Quartet is a credit Edison used for a mixed-voice ensemble of its house singers, overlapping heavily in personnel and repertoire with the Edison Mixed Quartet. Records under this name are typically hymns, sacred part-songs and unaccompanied arrangements.

It is kept as a separate entry because it is what appears on the label, and cataloguers need to be able to record the credit as printed rather than silently resolving it to another group.

people.name: Knickerbocker Quartet
people.summary: Male vocal quartet recording roughly 1910–1917, heard on cylinders in sentimental ballads and sacred material.
people.biography:
The Knickerbocker Quartet was one of the many male vocal groups assembled from the New York studio pool during the 1910s, recording between about 1910 and 1917. Its repertoire was the standard quartet fare of the period: old favourites such as "The Old Oaken Bucket," sacred numbers, and sentimental part-songs.

Groups of this kind were often the same handful of singers under a different name for a different label, and the Knickerbocker credit is best understood as a label identity rather than a fixed act. It appears on four-minute cylinders as well as on discs.

people.name: Sterling Trio
people.summary: Henry Burr, Albert Campbell and John H. Meyer — the standard male trio of the late acoustic era.
people.biography:
The Sterling Trio was formed from three members of the Peerless Quartet: the tenors Henry Burr and Albert Campbell with the bass John H. Meyer. It recorded from the mid-1910s into the 1920s, principally for Victor and Columbia but also for Edison and the smaller labels.

The three-voice texture — two tenors above a bass, without a baritone — gave a lighter, more transparent sound than the quartets, and the trio specialised in the sentimental ballad and the wartime song. Henry Moeller replaced Burr in 1926. Their material reached four-minute cylinder buyers through Edison and Indestructible issues.

people.name: Shannon Four
people.summary: Male quartet formed in 1917 — Charles Hart, Harvey Hindermyer, Elliott Shaw and Wilfred Glenn — which became the Shannon Quartet and then the Revelers.
people.biography:
The Shannon Four was organised in 1917 with tenors Charles Hart and Harvey Hindermyer, baritone Elliott Shaw and bass Wilfred Glenn. Lewis James replaced Hindermyer in 1918. The group was created partly to meet Victor's need for a second working male quartet alongside the Orpheus Quartet, and it quickly became one of the busiest ensembles in the studios.

After 1922 it was generally billed as the Shannon Quartet; in 1925 the name changed again, and by 1926 the group had become the **Revelers**, whose smooth, jazz-inflected close harmony was enormously influential in America and, through their European tours, on groups such as the Comedian Harmonists.

Their acoustic-era work reached four-minute cylinder buyers on Edison Blue Amberols dubbed from Diamond Disc masters, in the format's final years.

people.name: Orpheus Quartet
people.summary: Victor's house male quartet from 1911 to 1922, drawn from the same pool of singers as the other studio groups.
people.biography:
The Orpheus Quartet recorded from 1911 to about 1922, chiefly for Victor, where it served as the in-house male quartet alongside the American Quartet. Harry Macdonough sang with it, as did Lambert Murphy, Reinald Werrenrath and William F. Hooley at various points.

Its repertoire leaned to the serious end of the quartet trade: sacred music, art-song arrangements, old favourites and part-songs rather than comic novelties. Records under the name appear on four-minute cylinders as well as discs.

people.name: Edison Concert Band
people.summary: Edison's own studio band, the workhorse of the company's instrumental catalogue from the 1900s through the four-minute era.
people.biography:
The Edison Concert Band was the National Phonograph Company's house brass and reed band, made up of New York freelance players working under a series of studio conductors. Bands recorded better than anything else in the acoustic period — loud, brassy and full of the transients the horn could catch — so a band record was the standard demonstration piece for a new machine, and every catalogue carried dozens.

The Edison Concert Band supplied marches, overtures, medleys, dances and descriptive novelties across the whole run of Edison cylinders, including a large body of four-minute Amberol and Blue Amberol issues. Under related billings — Edison Military Band, New York Military Band, National Promenade Band — much the same personnel served different repertoire categories. Its records are among the easiest four-minute cylinders to find and, when in good condition, among the most impressive things to play on an Amberola.

people.name: Edison Military Band
people.summary: The Edison house band under its military billing, used for marches, patriotic selections and descriptive pieces.
people.biography:
Edison Military Band is one of the several names the company used for its studio band, applied particularly to marches, patriotic numbers and descriptive military pieces such as battle scenes with bugle calls and effects. The players overlapped substantially with the Edison Concert Band and the New York Military Band.

The distinction between these house-band credits was a matter of catalogue presentation rather than personnel, which is why a collector will see the same conductor's arrangements attributed to two or three different band names within a single supplement. The credit is recorded as printed.

people.name: New York Military Band
people.summary: Edison studio band credit of the Amberol and Blue Amberol years, prolific in marches and popular medleys.
people.biography:
The New York Military Band was one of the Edison studio band identities of the 1910s, recording marches, one-steps, medleys and popular selections for Amberol and Blue Amberol cylinders and for Diamond Discs. Like the Edison Concert Band and the Edison Military Band, it drew on the same pool of New York players.

Band records of this kind carried the popular hits of the day to buyers who wanted the tune without the words, and they make up a large share of any four-minute cylinder catalogue.

people.name: National Promenade Band
people.summary: Edison's dance-band billing of the mid-1910s, supplying one-steps, fox trots, waltzes and hesitations for home dancing.
people.biography:
The National Promenade Band was the name Edison put on its dance records during the ballroom craze that swept America from about 1913, when Vernon and Irene Castle made social dancing respectable and every household with a phonograph wanted a one-step.

The band recorded fox trots, one-steps, hesitation waltzes, tangos and maxixes for Blue Amberol and Diamond Disc, often with the dance type printed prominently on the label so a buyer could choose by step rather than by tune. Four-minute playing time was a genuine selling point here: a two-minute cylinder was over before a dance had properly begun.

people.name: American Symphony Orchestra
people.summary: Edison's house orchestra credit for light-classical and overture repertoire on four-minute cylinders and Diamond Discs.
people.biography:
The American Symphony Orchestra was an Edison studio ensemble billing rather than a concert orchestra — a pick-up group of New York players recording overtures, light classics, intermezzos and operatic selections for the company's more serious instrumental list.

Orchestral recording was the hardest problem in acoustic engineering: strings were weak, low instruments barely registered, and players had to crowd around the horn in unnatural arrangements, with Stroh violins and tubas substituting for double basses. The results are compromised by modern standards but were sold as the height of fidelity, and the four-minute cylinder allowed a whole overture where a two-minute one had allowed only an excerpt.
people.notes: Not connected with the later concert organisation of the same name founded in New York in 1962.

people.name: Sousa's Band
people.summary: John Philip Sousa's touring band, the most famous musical organisation in America and a staple of every cylinder catalogue.
people.biography:
Sousa's Band was formed in 1892 when John Philip Sousa left the United States Marine Band to go into business for himself, and for the next forty years it was the most celebrated musical organisation in the country, touring relentlessly at home and abroad and playing to audiences that no orchestra could match.

Its recording history is complicated, and worth understanding. Sousa himself distrusted recording — he coined the phrase "canned music" and wrote an essay attacking "The Menace of Mechanical Music" — and he very rarely conducted for the horn in person. The great majority of records credited to Sousa's Band were made by the band's players under other conductors, notably Arthur Pryor and Walter B. Rogers. That does not make them less valuable; they are the best surviving evidence of how the band actually sounded.

Sousa's Band records appear across the whole cylinder era, including four-minute Amberol and Blue Amberol issues and the celluloid cylinders of Indestructible and U-S Everlasting. Marches dominate, but the band's real repertoire was far broader — overtures, operatic transcriptions, novelties and popular selections of every kind.

people.name: Arthur Pryor's Band
people.summary: The band Arthur Pryor formed in 1903 after leaving Sousa, and one of the most heavily recorded ensembles of the acoustic era.
people.biography:
Arthur Pryor formed his own band in 1903, having spent a decade as Sousa's trombone soloist and principal recording conductor. He understood the recording horn better than almost anyone alive, and Pryor's Band became one of the most prolific recording organisations in America, working chiefly for Victor but issued widely elsewhere.

The band's repertoire ran from marches and Pryor's own compositions — "The Whistler and His Dog" above all — to ragtime, cakewalks, overtures and descriptive novelties. Pryor was an early and enthusiastic recorder of syncopated music, and his band's ragtime sides are important documents in their own right.

Pryor's Band recordings reached four-minute cylinder buyers through Indestructible and other licensed issues as well as through disc. He led the band until 1933.

people.name: Jaudas' Society Orchestra
people.summary: Edison dance orchestra of the 1910s, directed by Eugene Jaudas, recording fox trots, one-steps and waltzes.
people.biography:
Jaudas' Society Orchestra was an Edison house dance band of the 1910s, directed by the violinist and conductor Eugene A. Jaudas, who was one of the company's principal studio musicians. It recorded the ballroom repertoire of the period — one-steps, fox trots, hesitation waltzes, maxixes and tangos — for Blue Amberol cylinder and Diamond Disc.

The orchestra's name evokes the fashionable hotel and society dance bands that the recording companies were competing to imitate, and its records document the transitional moment between the ragtime dance craze and the arrival of jazz.

people.name: Irving Berlin
people.summary: The most important American songwriter of the twentieth century, whose 'Alexander's Ragtime Band' was one of the biggest-selling records of the cylinder era.
people.biography:
Israel Beilin was born in the Russian Empire in 1888 and brought to New York's Lower East Side as a child. He worked as a singing waiter in Chinatown, published his first song in 1907, and in 1911 wrote "Alexander's Ragtime Band," which sold sheet music by the million and became — in the Collins and Harlan recording and many others — one of the defining records of the four-minute cylinder period.

He could not read music properly and composed at a transposing piano, and he wrote both words and music, which was unusual. Between 1910 and 1930 his songs saturate the cylinder catalogues: "Everybody's Doin' It Now," "When I Lost You," "Oh! How I Hate to Get Up in the Morning," "A Pretty Girl Is Like a Melody," "Say It with Music," "All By Myself." Later came "Blue Skies," "God Bless America," "White Christmas" and *Annie Get Your Gun*.

He lived to 101, dying in 1989. On a four-minute cylinder label his name appears in parentheses after the title more often than almost any other composer's.

people.name: George M. Cohan
people.summary: Songwriter, playwright and performer whose flag-waving Broadway numbers were Billy Murray's staple repertoire and a mainstay of the cylinder catalogue.
people.biography:
George M. Cohan was born in Providence, Rhode Island, in 1878 into a vaudeville family and grew up on the road with the Four Cohans. He became the dominant figure of the early American musical stage: writer, composer, lyricist, director, producer and star, with more than three hundred songs and thirty musicals to his name.

His songs — "The Yankee Doodle Boy," "Give My Regards to Broadway," "You're a Grand Old Flag," "Mary's a Grand Old Name," "Harrigan" and, in 1917, "Over There" — are brash, rhythmically square, unashamedly patriotic and perfectly built for the acoustic recording horn. Billy Murray recorded most of them, and they appear on four-minute cylinders in quantity.

Cohan himself recorded comparatively little; his stage presence did not transfer well. He received a Congressional Gold Medal for "Over There" and "You're a Grand Old Flag" and died in 1942.

people.name: John Philip Sousa
people.summary: The March King — composer of 'The Stars and Stripes Forever' and leader of the most famous band in America, and a public opponent of recorded music.
people.biography:
John Philip Sousa was born in Washington, D.C., in 1854, led the United States Marine Band from 1880 to 1892, and then formed his own touring band. His marches — "The Stars and Stripes Forever," "Semper Fidelis," "The Washington Post," "El Capitan," "The Liberty Bell" — are among the most recorded pieces of music in existence, and they were a fixture of every cylinder catalogue from the 1890s onward.

His relationship with the phonograph was hostile. In 1906 he published "The Menace of Mechanical Music," arguing that canned music would destroy amateur music-making in the home and coarsen public taste, and he testified before Congress on composers' rights, helping to bring about the mechanical royalty provisions of the 1909 Copyright Act. He almost never conducted for the recording horn himself, and records billed as Sousa's Band were generally directed by Arthur Pryor or Walter B. Rogers.

He died in 1932. His compositions appear as composer credits on four-minute cylinders far more often than his own conducting does.

people.name: Arthur Pryor
people.summary: Trombone virtuoso, bandleader, composer of 'The Whistler and His Dog', and the man who conducted most of the records credited to Sousa's Band.
people.biography:
Arthur Pryor was born in St Joseph, Missouri, in 1870, the son of a bandmaster, and became the outstanding trombone soloist of his age — a player whose slide technique and range were considered barely credible by his contemporaries. He joined Sousa's Band in 1892, became its assistant conductor, and directed the great majority of its recording sessions, since Sousa himself would not.

In 1903 he formed Arthur Pryor's Band and built one of the most prolific recording organisations in America. He was also a composer of real charm: "The Whistler and His Dog" is his best-known piece, and he wrote a large body of marches, novelties and cakewalks.

Pryor understood the recording process as well as anyone in the business, and his sessions are consistently better balanced than those of conductors who treated the horn as an inconvenience. His compositions and conducting both turn up regularly on four-minute cylinders. He died in 1942.

people.name: Victor Herbert
people.summary: The leading American operetta composer of the period, whose selections filled the light-classical shelves of every cylinder catalogue.
people.biography:
Victor August Herbert was born in Dublin in 1859, trained as a cellist in Germany, and came to New York in 1886. He conducted the Pittsburgh Symphony, wrote two cello concertos and two grand operas, and became the dominant figure in American operetta with *Babes in Toyland*, *Mlle. Modiste*, *The Red Mill* and *Naughty Marietta*.

His songs — "Kiss Me Again," "Ah! Sweet Mystery of Life," "Gypsy Love Song," "Toyland" — were recorded constantly, and orchestral selections from his operettas were a staple of the four-minute cylinder, which for the first time gave a medley room to breathe. He was also a founder of ASCAP in 1914 and fought hard for composers' performance rights.

He died in 1924. Herbert occupies the middle ground between the concert hall and Tin Pan Alley that the Edison catalogue, in particular, was designed to serve.

people.name: Harry Von Tilzer
people.summary: One of Tin Pan Alley's founding figures and its most prolific songwriter, with several thousand published songs to his name.
people.biography:
Harry Von Tilzer — born Aaron Gumbinsky in Detroit in 1872 — ran away with a circus as a boy, worked in burlesque, and arrived in New York to become one of the architects of the Tin Pan Alley system: the songwriter as industrial producer, turning out material to order and publishing it himself. He is often credited with coining the name Tin Pan Alley itself.

His hits include "A Bird in a Gilded Cage," "Wait 'Til the Sun Shines, Nellie," "I Want a Girl (Just Like the Girl That Married Dear Old Dad)" and "Down Where the Wurzburger Flows," and he wrote coon songs, waltz ballads, comic numbers and novelties by the thousand. His name appears in the composer credits of four-minute cylinders more often than most.

He founded the Harry Von Tilzer Music Publishing Company in 1902 and remained in business for decades. His brother Albert was also a successful songwriter. He died in 1946.

people.name: Albert Von Tilzer
people.summary: Composer of 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' and 'Put Your Arms Around Me, Honey', and Harry Von Tilzer's younger brother.
people.biography:
Albert Von Tilzer followed his elder brother Harry into music publishing and songwriting and had a career nearly as prolific. In 1908 he set Jack Norworth's lyric "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" — neither man had been to a baseball game — and produced what became the third most frequently sung song in America. Edward Meeker's 1908 Edison cylinder of it is in the National Recording Registry.

His other successes include "Put Your Arms Around Me, Honey," "I'll Be with You in Apple Blossom Time" and "Oh By Jingo!" He founded the York Music Company with his brother Jack and worked into the 1930s. He died in 1956.

people.name: Gus Edwards
people.summary: Songwriter and vaudeville impresario whose 'School Days' and 'By the Light of the Silvery Moon' were cylinder-era standards.
people.biography:
Gus Edwards was born in Germany in 1878 and brought to New York as a child. He worked as a boy singer, became a songwriter, and then built a second career as vaudeville's great discoverer of juvenile talent — his "School Days" revues launched Eddie Cantor, George Jessel, Groucho Marx and Walter Winchell among others.

As a composer he wrote "School Days" (1907), "By the Light of the Silvery Moon" (1909, with lyrics by Edward Madden), "In My Merry Oldsmobile" and "Sunbonnet Sue." All were recorded repeatedly and appear across the four-minute cylinder catalogues in solo, duet and quartet versions. He died in 1945.

people.name: Jean Schwartz
people.summary: Hungarian-born Tin Pan Alley composer, best known for 'Chinatown, My Chinatown' and 'Rock-a-Bye Your Baby with a Dixie Melody'.
people.biography:
Jean Schwartz was born in Budapest in 1878 and emigrated to New York as a boy, working as a song plugger and pianist before establishing himself as a composer. His long partnership with the lyricist William Jerome produced a string of hits, and he wrote for Broadway revues throughout the 1900s and 1910s.

"Chinatown, My Chinatown" (1910), "Bedelia" (1903) and "Rock-a-Bye Your Baby with a Dixie Melody" (1918) are his best-remembered songs; the first two in particular were recorded constantly on cylinder, and "Chinatown" became a jazz-band standard as well. He died in 1956.

people.name: Charles K. Harris
people.summary: Author of 'After the Ball', the song that created the modern sheet-music industry and remained a cylinder standard for thirty years.
people.biography:
Charles K. Harris was born in Poughkeepsie in 1867 and advertised himself in Milwaukee as "Banjoist and Song Writer — Songs Written to Order." In 1892 he wrote, published and promoted "After the Ball," a waltz ballad about a misunderstanding that ruins a life. It sold five million copies of sheet music, made him rich, and demonstrated to the whole trade that a single song could be an industry.

He wrote hundreds more sentimental narrative ballads — "Break the News to Mother," "Hello Central, Give Me Heaven" — in the same vein: a story told over three verses with a chorus that turns the knife. The four-minute cylinder was well suited to them, since a two-minute record had to cut verses that the story needed. He died in 1930.

people.name: Paul Dresser
people.summary: Composer of 'On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away' and one of the great sentimental balladeers of the 1890s, whose songs stayed in cylinder catalogues long after his death.
people.biography:
Paul Dresser was born in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 1857 — elder brother of the novelist Theodore Dreiser, who changed the spelling of the family name back. He worked in minstrel shows and medicine shows before becoming one of the most successful ballad composers of the 1890s.

"On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away" (1897) became the state song of Indiana; "My Gal Sal" and "Just Tell Them That You Saw Me" were nearly as popular. His songs are sentimental in the fullest Victorian sense, with a real melodic gift underneath, and they remained in the cylinder catalogues for decades after his death in poverty in 1906 — carried forward into the four-minute era in remade versions by Edison, Indestructible and others.

people.name: Ernest R. Ball
people.summary: Composer of 'When Irish Eyes Are Smiling', 'Mother Machree' and 'Let the Rest of the World Go By' — the Irish-American ballad's central figure.
people.biography:
Ernest R. Ball was born in Cleveland in 1878 and trained at the Cleveland Conservatory before going to New York as a vaudeville accompanist. In 1910 he began collaborating with the singer and lyricist Chauncey Olcott, and the results defined the Irish-American sentimental ballad for a century: "Mother Machree" (1910), "When Irish Eyes Are Smiling" (1912), "Too-Ra-Loo-Ra-Loo-Ral" being a Shannon song of the same school.

He wrote several hundred songs, of which "Love Me and the World Is Mine" and "Let the Rest of the World Go By" were also large sellers. His music was recorded relentlessly by the ballad tenors of the four-minute era — Manuel Romain, Walter Van Brunt, Henry Burr, Will Oakland — and Irish material was one of the strongest categories in every cylinder catalogue. He collapsed and died backstage in Santa Ana, California, in 1927.

people.name: Chauncey Olcott
people.summary: Irish-American stage tenor, author of 'My Wild Irish Rose' and lyricist of 'Mother Machree' and 'When Irish Eyes Are Smiling'.
people.biography:
Chauncey Olcott was born in Buffalo in 1858 and became the leading Irish romantic tenor of the American stage, starring in a long series of sentimental Irish plays for which he wrote much of the music himself. "My Wild Irish Rose" (1899) is his, and he supplied the lyrics for Ernest R. Ball's "Mother Machree" (1911) and "When Irish Eyes Are Smiling" (1912), the latter written for his show *The Isle o' Dreams*.

He recorded relatively little himself, but his songs were among the most frequently recorded of the period and appear throughout the four-minute cylinder catalogues in versions by the house tenors of Edison, Indestructible and U-S Everlasting. He died in Monte Carlo in 1932.

people.name: Jerome Kern
people.summary: The composer who brought melodic sophistication to the American musical, and whose songs appear on cylinders from 1914 onward.
people.biography:
Jerome Kern was born in New York in 1885 and studied in Germany before beginning work as a song plugger and rehearsal pianist. He first made his name interpolating songs into imported European shows, then in the Princess Theatre musicals of 1915–1918 helped invent the integrated American book musical. *Show Boat* (1927) was the culmination.

His early hits — "They Didn't Believe Me" (1914), "Look for the Silver Lining," "Till the Clouds Roll By" — were recorded during the four-minute cylinder's commercial life and appear on Blue Amberols and on Indestructible issues. Kern's harmonic vocabulary was richer than Tin Pan Alley's norm, and singers of the period sometimes struggled with it; the records are correspondingly interesting.

He wrote for Hollywood in the 1930s and 1940s and died in 1945.

people.name: Percy Wenrich
people.summary: Ragtime and popular composer from Joplin, Missouri — 'Put On Your Old Grey Bonnet', 'When You Wore a Tulip', 'Moonlight Bay'.
people.biography:
Percy Wenrich was born in Joplin, Missouri, in 1887 and was nicknamed "the Joplin Kid" — a happy coincidence, given Scott Joplin's association with the same town. He wrote instrumental rags early on, then moved into popular song and produced a run of hits that are still recognisable: "Put On Your Old Grey Bonnet" (1909), "Moonlight Bay" (1912) and "When You Wore a Tulip and I Wore a Big Red Rose" (1914).

All three were recorded repeatedly during the four-minute cylinder era, "Moonlight Bay" most famously by the American Quartet. Wenrich later performed in vaudeville with his wife Dolly Connolly, who introduced many of his songs. He died in 1952.

people.name: Egbert Van Alstyne
people.summary: Composer of 'In the Shade of the Old Apple Tree' and 'Memories', usually in partnership with the lyricist Harry Williams.
people.biography:
Egbert Van Alstyne was born in Chicago in 1878 and worked as a theatre pianist before forming a long and productive partnership with the lyricist Harry Williams. Their "In the Shade of the Old Apple Tree" (1905) was one of the biggest sellers of the decade and stayed in cylinder catalogues for twenty years; "Won't You Come Over to My House" and "I'm Afraid to Come Home in the Dark" followed.

Later, with Gus Kahn, he wrote "Memories" (1915) and "Pretty Baby" (1916). All of these were recorded extensively by the singers and quartets who filled the four-minute cylinder catalogues. He died in 1951.

people.name: Harry Williams
people.summary: Lyricist of 'In the Shade of the Old Apple Tree' and 'It's a Long, Long Way to Tipperary'-era standards, chiefly in partnership with Egbert Van Alstyne.
people.biography:
Harry Hiram Williams was born in 1879 and worked as a lyricist and publisher from 1903 until his death in 1922. His principal collaborator was the composer Egbert Van Alstyne, with whom he wrote "In the Shade of the Old Apple Tree," "Won't You Come Over to My House" and "I'm Afraid to Come Home in the Dark."

He also wrote "Mickey" and worked in the motion-picture business in his later years. His words appear in the lyricist credit of a great many four-minute cylinders from the format's most productive decade.

people.name: Theodore Morse
people.summary: Composer of 'M-O-T-H-E-R', 'Blue Bell' and 'Hail! Hail! The Gang's All Here', frequently in collaboration with his wife Theodora.
people.biography:
Theodore F. Morse was born in 1873 and became one of the reliable hit-makers of the Tin Pan Alley generation, often collaborating with his wife Theodora, who wrote lyrics under the name Dorothy Terriss (among others).

His songs include "Blue Bell" (1904), a Haydn Quartet favourite; "Dear Old Girl"; "Hail! Hail! The Gang's All Here"; and "M-O-T-H-E-R (A Word That Means the World to Me)" (1915), a spelling-out sentimental ballad that was recorded again and again during the Blue Amberol years. He died in 1924.

people.name: Fred Fisher
people.summary: German-born songwriter and publisher — 'Peg o' My Heart', 'Dardanella', 'Chicago' — and a fixture of the late cylinder-era repertoire.
people.biography:
Fred Fisher was born Alfred Breitenbach in Cologne in 1875, served in the German navy and the French Foreign Legion by his own account, and reached the United States in 1900. He anglicised his name — dropping the c during the First World War — and became a successful songwriter and publisher.

"Come, Josephine, in My Flying Machine" (1910) was an early hit and a Billy Murray and Ada Jones cylinder staple; "Peg o' My Heart" (1913), "There's a Broken Heart for Every Light on Broadway" (1915), "Dardanella" (1919) and "Chicago (That Toddlin' Town)" (1922) followed. He sued successfully over "Dardanella" in a landmark music-copyright case. He died in 1942.

people.name: Shelton Brooks
people.summary: Black Canadian-American composer of 'Some of These Days' and 'Darktown Strutters' Ball', two of the most recorded songs of the era.
people.biography:
Shelton Brooks was born in Amherstburg, Ontario, in 1886, to a family descended from people who had escaped slavery in the United States, and grew up in Detroit. He worked as a ragtime pianist and vaudeville comedian and wrote two songs that outlived nearly everything else from their moment.

"Some of These Days" (1910) became Sophie Tucker's lifelong theme song; "The Darktown Strutters' Ball" (1917) became one of the most recorded songs in American history and an early jazz standard. Both were taken up immediately by the recording companies and appear on four-minute cylinders as well as discs.

Brooks continued to perform into old age, appearing on television in the 1960s. He died in 1975.

people.name: Lewis F. Muir
people.summary: Ragtime pianist and composer of 'Waiting for the Robert E. Lee' and 'Ragtime Cowboy Joe', dead at thirty-two.
people.biography:
Lewis F. Muir was born on 30 May 1883 and worked as a ragtime pianist in St Louis and New York. With the lyricist L. Wolfe Gilbert he wrote "Waiting for the Robert E. Lee" (1912), one of the biggest hits of the pre-war years and a song recorded constantly on cylinder and disc; "Ragtime Cowboy Joe" (1912) and "Hitchy Koo" were nearly as successful.

His syncopated, singable style sat exactly where popular song and ragtime met, and his songs suited the loud, rhythmic delivery the acoustic horn rewarded. He died on 3 December 1915, aged thirty-two.

people.name: Kerry Mills
people.summary: Composer of 'At a Georgia Camp Meeting' and 'Meet Me in St. Louis, Louis', and a key figure in the cakewalk craze.
people.biography:
Frederick Allen Mills, who published as Kerry Mills, was a trained violinist and music teacher who turned to popular composition in the 1890s. "At a Georgia Camp Meeting" (1897) was among the most successful cakewalks ever written and became a standard test piece for bands, banjoists and, later, jazz musicians; "Whistling Rufus" followed.

In 1904 he wrote "Meet Me in St. Louis, Louis" for the World's Fair, and it became one of the most recorded songs of the decade. His cakewalks are ubiquitous in band and banjo cylinder catalogues, including four-minute issues, where the extra playing time allowed a fuller set of strains. He died in 1948.

people.name: Jack Norworth
people.summary: Vaudeville performer and lyricist of 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' and 'Shine On, Harvest Moon'.
people.biography:
Jack Norworth was a vaudeville headliner as well as a writer, and for a time was married to and performed with Nora Bayes. In 1908 he scribbled the words of "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" on a scrap of paper during a subway ride, having never attended a baseball game; Albert Von Tilzer set it, and it became one of the most sung songs in the English language.

With Bayes he wrote "Shine On, Harvest Moon" the same year — another permanent standard, recorded on cylinder by Ada Jones and Billy Murray among many others. Norworth wrote or co-wrote some 2,500 songs and lived until 1959.

people.name: Nora Bayes
people.summary: Vaudeville and Ziegfeld star, co-author of 'Shine On, Harvest Moon' and the first great recorded interpreter of 'Over There'.
people.biography:
Nora Bayes was one of the biggest stars American vaudeville produced — a commanding, wry, thoroughly modern performer who headlined the Ziegfeld Follies and toured to enormous fees. With her husband Jack Norworth she wrote "Shine On, Harvest Moon" in 1908, and the pair performed it together as a signature number.

She recorded for Victor and Columbia, and her 1917 recording of George M. Cohan's "Over There" was among the most important records of the war years. Her material circulated on four-minute cylinders through Columbia's Indestructible issues and in versions by other artists.

Bayes married five times, spent money as fast as she made it, and died of cancer in 1928 at forty-eight.

people.name: Sam M. Lewis
people.summary: Lyricist, almost always in partnership with Joe Young — 'Rock-a-Bye Your Baby with a Dixie Melody', 'How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm'.
people.biography:
Sam M. Lewis was born in New York in 1885 and formed with Joe Young one of the most productive lyric-writing partnerships of the 1910s and 1920s. Their credits include "Rock-a-Bye Your Baby with a Dixie Melody" (1918), "How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm (After They've Seen Paree?)" (1919), "I'm Sitting on Top of the World" (1925) and "Dinah" (1925).

The wartime and immediately post-war songs in particular were recorded heavily during the Blue Amberol period, and the Lewis and Young credit is a common sight on late four-minute cylinder labels. He died in 1959.

people.name: Joe Young
people.summary: Lyricist and Sam M. Lewis's inseparable partner, co-author of many of the biggest songs of the war and post-war years.
people.biography:
Joe Young was born in New York in 1889 and worked as a singer and song plugger before turning full time to lyric writing. His partnership with Sam M. Lewis produced a remarkable run of hits between about 1916 and 1930, and the two names appear together so consistently that they are effectively a single credit.

Among their songs are "Rock-a-Bye Your Baby with a Dixie Melody," "How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm," "Five Foot Two, Eyes of Blue" and "In a Shanty in Old Shanty Town." He died in 1939.

people.name: Walter Donaldson
people.summary: Composer of 'My Blue Heaven', 'Carolina in the Morning' and 'How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm', spanning the end of the cylinder era.
people.biography:
Walter Donaldson was born in Brooklyn in 1893 and became one of the most successful American songwriters of the 1920s. He wrote "How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm" (1919) with Lewis and Young while serving in the army, and followed it with "My Mammy," "Carolina in the Morning," "My Buddy," "Yes Sir, That's My Baby" and "My Blue Heaven."

His songs bridge the acoustic and electrical eras, and the earlier ones appear on late Edison Blue Amberol cylinders — among the last new popular material the four-minute format ever carried before its discontinuation in 1929. He died in 1947.

people.name: Geoffrey O'Hara
people.summary: Composer of 'K-K-K-Katy' and 'There Is No Death', and an early recordist of Native American music for the US government.
people.biography:
Geoffrey O'Hara was born in Chatham, Ontario, on 2 February 1882 and settled in the United States, where he wrote more than five hundred songs, hymns and choral works. In 1913 the federal government engaged him to make cylinder recordings of Native American music — an early and significant piece of ethnographic field recording.

His best-known song is the wartime novelty "K-K-K-Katy" (1918), a stammering-soldier number that Billy Murray recorded to enormous success and that reached cylinder buyers on Blue Amberol. He also wrote the sacred song "There Is No Death" and the popular "Give a Man a Horse He Can Ride." He taught, lectured and worked in music education for decades, and died in 1967.

people.name: Richard A. Whiting
people.summary: Composer of 'Till We Meet Again', one of the biggest-selling songs of the First World War, and later a Hollywood songwriter.
people.biography:
Richard A. Whiting was born in Peoria, Illinois, on 12 November 1891 and worked for the Detroit publisher Jerome H. Remick. In 1918, with the lyricist Raymond B. Egan, he wrote "Till We Meet Again," a waltz farewell that became one of the best-selling pieces of sheet music of the entire war and was recorded by practically every artist on every label, including on four-minute cylinders.

He went on to write "Ain't We Got Fun?", "Sleepy Time Gal," "Hooray for Hollywood" and "On the Good Ship Lollipop" for the films. He was the father of the singer Margaret Whiting, and died in 1938.

people.name: J. R. Shannon
people.summary: Composer of 'Too-Ra-Loo-Ra-Loo-Ral (That's an Irish Lullaby)' and lyricist of 'The Missouri Waltz'.
people.biography:
James Royce Shannon was born on 13 May 1881 and worked in Tin Pan Alley as both composer and lyricist. His "Too-Ra-Loo-Ra-Loo-Ral (That's an Irish Lullaby)," written in 1913 for the show *Shameen Dhu*, became one of the permanent fixtures of Irish-American sentiment and was recorded repeatedly during the Blue Amberol years.

He also supplied the lyrics to "The Missouri Waltz," later the state song of Missouri and a favourite of President Truman's. He died in 1946.

people.name: Ethelbert Nevin
people.summary: Composer of 'The Rosary' and 'Mighty Lak' a Rose', two of the most recorded American concert songs of the phonograph's first decades.
people.biography:
Ethelbert Nevin was born near Pittsburgh in 1862 and trained in Boston and Berlin. He wrote piano miniatures and songs in a refined salon style, and two of them became phenomena: "The Rosary" (1898), a setting of a poem by Robert Cameron Rogers that sold millions of copies of sheet music and was recorded by nearly every serious singer of the era, and "Mighty Lak' a Rose" (1901).

Both belong to the category the four-minute cylinder was ideally suited to — a full-length concert song sung with orchestra, requiring more than two minutes to do properly. Christine Miller's Edison recording of "The Rosary" is among the best known. Nevin died in 1901, aged only thirty-eight, before the phonograph made his songs universal.

people.name: Carrie Jacobs-Bond
people.summary: Composer of 'A Perfect Day' and 'I Love You Truly', and the first American woman to run her own successful music publishing business.
people.biography:
Carrie Jacobs-Bond was born in Janesville, Wisconsin, in 1862, was widowed young and left in poverty, and supported herself by painting china and writing songs. Unable to interest publishers, she founded her own firm, Carrie Jacobs-Bond & Son, in Chicago and made a fortune from it — the first American woman to succeed on that scale in music publishing.

"I Love You Truly" (1901) became the standard American wedding song; "A Perfect Day" (1910) sold something like eight million copies of sheet music and was recorded by everyone. Both are staples of the four-minute cylinder catalogue, sung by the house sopranos and quartets of Edison and its rivals. She died in 1946.

people.name: Stephen Foster
people.summary: The father of American popular song, dead half a century before the four-minute cylinder — and still one of the most frequently credited composers on its labels.
people.biography:
Stephen Collins Foster was born in Lawrenceville, Pennsylvania, in 1826 and wrote some two hundred songs before dying destitute in New York in 1864, aged thirty-seven. "Oh! Susanna," "Camptown Races," "My Old Kentucky Home," "Old Folks at Home," "Jeanie with the Light Brown Hair" and "Beautiful Dreamer" are his.

He belongs in a four-minute cylinder register because his songs never left the catalogue. Long out of copyright, endlessly arranged for quartet, band, banjo, xylophone and solo voice, they were the safest possible repertoire for a record company: universally known, requiring no royalty, and acceptable to every kind of customer. Edison, Indestructible, U-S Everlasting and Columbia all issued Foster titles on four-minute cylinders, often in multiple versions.

Much of his output was written for the minstrel stage and carries its dialect and its assumptions, though Foster took the unusual step of softening or removing caricature in later revisions of his own songs. The melodic gift is not in dispute; his place in the four-minute catalogue is simply enormous.
